'''Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport''' {{airport codes|UPG|WAAA}} is an [[international airport]] serving [[Makassar]], [[South Sulawesi]], [[Indonesia]]. The airport is located on the border between Makassar and [[Maros]], a suburb in South Sulawesi, approximately 20 km (12 mi) or 15 minutes from Makassar city center via the freeway/tollway, and about 23 km (14 mi) or 20 minutes via the highway. Named after [[Hasanuddin of Gowa|Sultan Hasanuddin]] (1631–1670), the [[Sultanate of Gowa|Sultan of Gowa]] and a [[National Hero of Indonesia|national hero of Indonesia]] who resisted the [[Dutch East India Company]] in the 1660s, the airport serves as the main gateway to [[eastern Indonesia]] and is a major aviation hub in the region. It is the largest airport in eastern Indonesia and one of only three international airports in [[Sulawesi]]. The airport serves as a key hub connecting western and eastern Indonesia, offering domestic flights to major cities in western Indonesia such as [[Jakarta]], [[Surabaya]], [[Denpasar]], and [[Balikpapan]], as well as destinations in eastern Indonesia, including [[Ambon, Maluku|Ambon]], [[Ternate]], [[Sorong]], and [[Jayapura]]. It also provides international connections to destinations such as [[Singapore]] and [[Malaysia]]. Additionally, the airport is one of the primary embarkation points for [[Hajj]] pilgrims from eastern Indonesia, with seasonal flights to [[Jeddah]] and [[Medina]].

In addition to serving as a commercial airport, Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport also hosts the '''Sultan Hasanuddin Air Force Base''', a Type-A facility operated by the [[Indonesian Air Force]]. It is one of the largest air force bases in eastern Indonesia and is home to four Air Force squadrons: the 5th Reconnaissance Squadron, which operates [[Boeing 737|Boeing 737-200]] and [[CASA/IPTN CN-235|CN 235-220]] aircraft; the 11th Combat Squadron, equipped with [[Sukhoi Su-27]] and [[Sukhoi Su-30|Su-30]] fighter jets; the 33rd Transport Squadron, which flies [[Lockheed C-130 Hercules|Lockheed C-130H Hercules]] aircraft; and the 044th Engineering Squadron.

==History==

=== Colonial era ===
[[File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM Vliegtuigen van Skyways International en de KLM op het vliegveld van Makassar TMnr 10029499.jpg|thumb|left|A [[Curtiss C-46 Commando]] at Mandai Airfield, 1948]]
Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport was first built by the [[Dutch East Indies|Dutch colonial government]] in 1935 and was originally known as Kadieng Airfield. After approximately two years of construction, the Dutch government officially opened the airport on 27 September 1937, marked by a commercial flight connecting [[Singapore]] using a [[Douglas DC-2]] aircraft operated by the [[KNILM|Koninklijke Nederlands Indische Luchtvaart Maatschappij]] (KNILM).<ref>{{Cite web |last=AP |first=Bahar |date=2023-12-04 |title=Dibangun Belanda Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Beberapa Kali Berganti Nama |url=https://www.marosnews.com/dibangun-belanda-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-beberapa-kali-berganti-nama/ |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=Maros News |language=id}}</ref> At the time of its inauguration, the airfield had only a single grass runway measuring 1,600 × 45 meters.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Halimsyah |first=Ilham |date=2012-04-10 |title=Bandara Internasional Sultan Hasanuddin Terletak di Maros |url=https://www.kompasiana.com/catatanilham/550f4139a33311aa2dba8359/bandara-internasional-sultan-hasanuddin-terletak-di-maros |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=KOMPASIANA |language=id}}</ref>

The airfield was considered strategically important by the [[Empire of Japan|Japanese]] during the opening phase of the [[Pacific War|Pacific Theater]] of [[World War II]], as it enabled them to launch air offensives against targets in [[Java]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Lohnstein |first=Marc |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/The_Netherlands_East_Indies_Campaign_194/26UhEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=makassar+airfield+japanese&pg=PA51&printsec=frontcover |title=The Netherlands East Indies Campaign 1941–42: Japan's Quest for Oil |date=2021-06-24 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-4728-4354-8 |pages=51 |language=en}}</ref> Around midnight on 8–9 February 1942, Japanese troops landed in Makassar. Realizing the hopelessness of the situation, the Dutch commander in Sulawesi, Colonel M. Vooren, based his defensive strategy on the [[Malayan campaign]].<ref name=":3" /> His objective was to inflict the greatest possible losses on the enemy while delaying their advance for as long as possible.<ref name=":3" /> To achieve this, he abandoned the conventional doctrine of direct coastal defence in favour of an indirect defensive strategy: slowing the enemy advance to facilitate the planned destruction of Mandai Airfield, before making a final stand at the Tjamba position in the mountainous interior. The entire plan was purely defensive.<ref name=":3" /> The city and the destroyed airfield were occupied by Japanese forces around noon on 9 February 1942. The Japanese later rebuilt the airfield during their [[Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies|occupation]] from 1942 to 1945, including upgrading its grass runway to a concrete surface. The rehabilitation work involved [[Allied prisoners of war of Japan|Allied prisoners of war]], who were subjected to harsh treatment by their captors.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Romeiser |first=John |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/The_East_Tennessee_Veterans_Memorial/1qOTEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=mandai+airfield&pg=PT104&printsec=frontcover |title=The East Tennessee Veterans Memorial: A Pictorial History of the Names on the Wall, Their Service, and Their Sacrifice |last2=McCall |first2=Jack H. |date=2026-04-07 |publisher=University of Tennessee Press |isbn=979-8-89527-242-8 |language=en}}</ref> Some Allied prisoners were executed by Japanese forces throughout the occupation, continuing until the end of the war.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Administration |first=United States National Archives and Records |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/Japanese_War_Crimes_and_Related_Topics_A/Gx9JDwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=maros+airfield&pg=PA848&printsec=frontcover |title=Japanese War Crimes and Related Topics: A Guide to Records at the National Archives |date=2007 |publisher=Jeffrey Frank Jones |pages=848 |language=en}}</ref> During this period, the airfield was renamed Mandai Airfield.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Saminja |first=Suhandi |date=15 December 2023 |title=Sejarah Unik Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin, Pernah Ganti Nama Empat Kali, Apa Saja? |url=https://sulsel.herald.id/2023/12/15/sejarah-unik-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-pernah-ganti-nama-empat-kali-apa-saja/ |website=Sulsel Herald |language=id}}</ref> Throughout the war, the airfield was repeatedly targeted by Allied air raids.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lawless |first=Richard Phillip |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/Nightstalkers/_RmsEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=mandai+airfield+japanese&pg=PA243&printsec=frontcover |title=Nightstalkers: The Wright Project and the 868th Bomb Squadron in World War II |date=2023-02-23 |publisher=Casemate |isbn=978-1-63624-206-4 |pages=243 |language=en}}</ref> By the end of the war, the airfield was in poor condition due to [[Allies of World War II|Allied]] bombing, with the runway heavily cratered.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Sandes |first=E. W. C. |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/The_Indian_Engineers_1939_47/lhhq1lygnq4C?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=mandai+airfield+japanese&dq=mandai+airfield+japanese&printsec=frontcover |title=The Indian Engineers, 1939-47 |date=1956 |publisher=Institution of Royal Engineers |pages=456 |language=en}}</ref> It was subsequently repaired by Australian and Indian engineers,<ref name=":4" /> after which Allied forces extended the runway to 1,745 × 45 meters.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Quraisy |first=Muhammad Ibrahim |date=28 March 2017 |title=Sejarah Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Dulu dan Sekarang |url=https://www.bagooli.com |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=Bagooli |language=id}}</ref> The construction involved approximately 4,000 workers, including former [[Japanese prisoners of war in World War II|Japanese prisoners of war]].<ref name=":1" />

With the end of the war, the airfield was handed over to the returning Dutch authorities. It was subsequently used as an airbase by the [[Royal Netherlands East Indies Army Air Force]] (ML-KNIL) during the [[Indonesian National Revolution]] until 1950.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/Sejarah_TNI_Angkatan_Udara_1950_1959/A29fkH3ixJkC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=lapangan+terbang+mandai&pg=PA32&printsec=frontcover |title=Sejarah TNI Angkatan Udara: 1950-1959 |date=2004 |publisher=Subdisjarah Diswatpersau |pages=32 |language=id}}</ref> During the [[Makassar Uprising]] in April 1950, negotiations were held at the airfield between [[Martinus Putuhena]], [[Cabinet of the State of East Indonesia|Prime Minister of the State of East Indonesia]]; Colonel [[Alex Kawilarang]] of the [[Indonesian Army]]; and Major General Schaffelaar of the [[Royal Netherlands East Indies Army]] (KNIL), in an effort to end the uprising by disgruntled former KNIL soldiers.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Penerangan |first=Indonesia Departemen |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/Propinsi_Sulawesi/cnMSAAAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=lapangan+terbang+mandai&pg=PA316&printsec=frontcover |title=Propinsi Sulawesi |date=1953 |publisher=Kementerian Penerangan |pages=316 |language=id}}</ref>

=== Post-independence era ===
[[File:Makasar Anfahrt.jpg|thumb|left|Exterior of the former terminal, which was destroyed by fire in 2016]]
Following the [[Dutch-Indonesian Round Table Conference|Dutch recognition of Indonesia's sovereignty]], Dutch forces withdrew from Makassar, and control of the airfield was transferred from the ML-KNIL to the [[Indonesian Air Force]] on 2 June 1950.<ref name=":5" /> Its operation and maintenance were initially jointly managed by the Indonesian Air Force and the Airfield Division of the Department of Public Work.<ref name=":5" /> During this period, the airport became one of the busiest in the country, serving as a vital link between western and eastern Indonesia. In 1955, the airport's management was transferred to the Civil Aviation Service, now known as the [[Directorate General of Civil Aviation (Indonesia)|Directorate General of Civil Aviation]]. The runway was subsequently extended to 2,345 × 45 meters.<ref name=":1" /> The airfield was bombed on 13 April 1958 by U.S.-supplied [[Douglas A-26 Invader]] aircraft operated by the Permesta Air Force (AUREV), based in [[North Sulawesi]], during the height of the [[Permesta]] rebellion.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/Monthly_Indonesian_Press_Survey/ipcdopKVirEC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=mandai+airfield&pg=RA3-PA43&printsec=frontcover |title=Monthly Indonesian Press Survey |date=1958 |publisher=External Research Division, Bureau of Intelligence and Research. |pages=43 |language=en}}</ref> 

In 1962, an assassination attempt on President [[Sukarno]], who was visiting Makassar, was carried out at the airfield by the [[Darul Islam rebellion|Darul Islam]] movement led by [[Abdul Kahar Muzakkar]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Saelan |first=Maulwi |url=https://www.google.co.id/books/edition/Dari_Revolusi_45_sampai_Kudeta_66/nXzHkVr4YmEC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=lapangan+terbang+mandai&pg=PA176&printsec=frontcover |title=Dari Revolusi 45 sampai Kudeta 66: kesaksian Wakil Komandan Tjakrabirawa |date=2008 |publisher=VisiMedia |isbn=978-979-1043-99-1 |pages=176 |language=id}}</ref> Mortars were fired at his motorcade as it exited Mandai Airfield; fortunately, the rounds missed by a considerable margin.<ref name=":6" />

In 1980, the airport was renamed to its present name in honor of [[Hasanuddin of Gowa|Sultan Hasanuddin]], the 17th-century ruler of the [[Sultanate of Gowa|Gowa Sultanate]] who famously resisted Dutch colonial forces in South Sulawesi. The renaming coincided with a runway extension from 1,745 × 45 meters to 2,400 × 45 meters. The following year, the airport began serving as a [[Hajj]] embarkation point, operating regular flights on the Makassar–[[Jeddah]] route to accommodate pilgrims traveling to [[Mecca]]. Sultan Hasanuddin Airport experienced a significant rise in passenger traffic and international arrivals after the issuance of Minister of Transportation Decree No. KM 61/1994 on 30 October 1994, which officially granted it international status. The airport's first regular international route was inaugurated on 28 March 1995 with the launch of the Makassar–[[Kuala Lumpur]] service by [[Malaysia Airlines]], followed soon after by [[SilkAir]]’s route to [[Singapore]].<ref name=":1" /> However, between 28 October 2006 and mid-2008, all international routes to Makassar were temporarily suspended after [[Garuda Indonesia]] closed the Makassar–Singapore route due to substantial financial losses. This decision mirrored the earlier moves by Malaysia Airlines and SilkAir, both of which had also discontinued their services to Makassar.<ref name=":1" /> International service resumed shortly afterwards.

Following the opening of the new terminal in 2008, located 2 km from the old terminal, the latter was closed to the public and repurposed for use by the [[Indonesian Air Force]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=4 August 2008 |title=Bandara Hasanuddin Makassar Pindah Tempat |url=https://news.detik.com/berita/d-982588/bandara-hasanuddin-makassar-pindah-tempat |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=detiknews |language=id-ID}}</ref> On 15 August 2016, the old terminal building was destroyed in a major fire.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Setiawan |first=Agus |date=15 August 2016 |title=Terminal Lama Bandara Hasanuddin Terbakar |url=https://babel.antaranews.com/berita/41147/terminal-lama-bandara-hasanuddin-terbakar? |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=ANTARA News Bangka Belitung |language=id}}</ref>

This airport has earned recognition as one of the top three airports in Indonesia, winning awards in 2011 for excellence in service and having the cleanest toilets. In 2012, it received the highest honor from the [[Ministry of Transportation (Indonesia)|Ministry of Transportation]], winning the Airport Award as the best airport.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bagooli.com/sejarah-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-dulu-dan-sekarang/ | title=Sejarah Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Dulu dan Sekarang | date=28 March 2017 }}</ref>

==Facilities and development==
[[File:Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport 2024.jpg|thumb|Check-in area after the 2024 expansion]]
[[File:Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport Terminal.jpg|thumb|Boarding gate]]
The current terminal, located approximately 2 kilometers south of the old facility, began operations on 4 August 2008 and was officially inaugurated by President [[Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono]] on 26 September 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 September 2008 |title=Presiden Resmikan Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin dan Jalan Tol |url=https://otomotif.kompas.com/read/2008/09/26/10144916/presiden.resmikan.bandara.sultan.hasanuddin.dan.jalan.tol.html |website=[[Kompas]] |language=id}}</ref> Construction, which started in 2004, took around four years to complete. The project was carried out together with the 11.47 kilometer extension of the Ujung Pandang Tollway, improving access between the airport, Makassar city center, and the [[Port of Makassar]]. It also included the construction of a new runway measuring 3,100 by 45 meters.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Suryanto |date=2008-09-09 |title=Presiden Resmikan Bandara dan Jalan Tol di Makassar |url=https://www.antaranews.com/berita/116068/@antarajatimcom |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=Antara News |language=id}}</ref> The airport building features a futuristic architectural style, dominated by glass wall elements and complemented by ornaments from South Sulawesi.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 September 2008 |title=Presiden SBY Resmikan Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Makassar |url=https://news.detik.com/berita/d-1012840/presiden-sby-resmikan-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-makassar |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=detiknews |language=id-ID}}</ref> The ten roof arches are interpreted as waves, symbolizing the spirit of the [[Bugis]] and [[Makassar people]], who are known worldwide as resilient seafarers.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=Ariwibowo |first=A. A. |date=2008-09-26 |title=Bandara Internasional Sultan Hasanuddin Diresmikan |url=https://www.antaranews.com/berita/118494/bandara-internasional-sultan-hasanuddin-diresmikan |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=Antara News |language=id}}</ref> A traditional Bugis ''[[Pinisi|Phinisi]]'' ship is depicted on the main arch pillars, while the terminal ceiling incorporates motifs inspired by [[Mandarese people|Mandar]] embroidered textiles.<ref name=":7" /> It is five times larger than the previous terminal and has a capacity of seven million passengers per year. By 2010, it was already serving five million passengers.<ref>{{cite web |author=Oleh Edy Can |date=28 July 2011 |title=4 of Indonesia's Main Airports Bursting at Seams: Official|url=http://english.kontan.co.id/v2/read/1311832305/74030/4-of-Indonesias-main-airports-bursting-at-seams-Official |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110815174413/http://english.kontan.co.id/v2/read/1311832305/74030/4-of-Indonesias-main-airports-bursting-at-seams-Official |archive-date=15 August 2011 |access-date=12 July 2013 |publisher=Kontan }}</ref> The terminal includes six aerobridges and a significantly larger apron that can accommodate up to seventeen [[wide-body aircraft]]. The total cost for the terminal and supporting infrastructure was approximately more than 600 billion rupiah.<ref name=":7" />

Due to overcapacity, with approximately 10.7 million passengers passing through the airport in 2019 despite its original design for only 7 million, a major expansion project was launched in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Busthomi |date=2020-09-30 |title=AP I Kebut Perluasan Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Makassar |url=https://www.topbusiness.id/41244/ap-i-kebut-perluasan-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-makassar.html |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=TopBusiness |language=id}}</ref> The project aimed to boost the airport's annual capacity to 15.5 million passengers and to triple the terminal's size from 50,000 to 150,000 square meters. The expansion was divided into two main components. The first included the revitalization of the existing terminal, a southern extension, the construction of a multi-level parking facility, and improvements to the main access road. The second involved the development of new aircraft aprons on the southern and eastern sides of the airport, along with supporting infrastructure.<ref>{{Cite web |last=A.S |first=Anastasia |date=6 October 2020 |title=Pemerintah Targetkan Pembangunan Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Makassar Selesai Oktober 2021 |url=https://swa.co.id/read/276377/pemerintah-targetkan-pembangunan-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-makassar-selesai-oktober-2021 |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=swa.co.id |language=id}}</ref> As part of the project, the apron was expanded to accommodate 37 aircraft stands, up from 34, and the parking area was enlarged from 40 to 72 square meters.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Praditya |first=Ilyas Istianur |date=27 September 2019 |editor=Nurmayanti |title=Kemenhub Bakal Perluas Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Tiga Kali Lipat |url=https://www.liputan6.com/bisnis/read/4072931/kemenhub-bakal-perluas-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-tiga-kali-lipat |work=[[Liputan6.com]]}}</ref> The number of jet bridges at the airport was increased from six to twelve.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hidayah |first=Nurul |date=4 December 2023 |title=Perluasan Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Sudah 68 Persen, Ditarget Rampung Akhir 2024 |url=https://makassar.tribunnews.com/2023/12/04/perluasan-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-sudah-68-persen-ditarget-rampung-akhir-2024 |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=Tribun-timur.com |language=id-ID}}</ref> The total cost of the expansion was estimated at 2.4 trillion rupiah.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hidayah |first=Nurul |date=3 April 2024 |title=Total Anggaran Perluasan Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Rp2,4 Triliun, Progres Pembangunan Baru 73 Persen |url=https://makassar.tribunnews.com/2024/04/03/total-anggaran-perluasan-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-rp24-triliun-progres-pembangunan-baru-73-persen |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=Tribun-timur.com |language=id-ID}}</ref> Originally slated for completion in 2021, the project was delayed and was briefly halted due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], with construction resuming in 2023. The expanded terminal was completed and officially opened to the public on 26 June 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 June 2024 |title=Terminal Baru Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Makassar Beroperasi 26 Juni |url=https://www.detik.com/sulsel/makassar/d-7407178/terminal-baru-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-makassar-beroperasi-26-juni |access-date=2025-05-05 |website=detiksulsel |language=id-ID}}</ref>

The airport is planned to undergo further expansion in four phases. The first phase has been completed and became operational in 2024. Phase II was originally scheduled to begin in 2024, increasing the airport's passenger capacity to 21 million per year and expanding the number of parking stands to 47. Phase III, set to commence in 2034, will raise the terminal capacity to 30.8 million passengers annually with 64 parking stands. Finally, Phase IV will begin in 2044, bringing the terminal's ultimate capacity to 40 million passengers per year and 78 parking stands.<ref name=":2" />

== Ground transport ==

=== Bus ===
[[Perum DAMRI]] operates a bus service from Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport to Tanjung Bira Beach in [[Bulukumba Regency]].<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Yustika |first=Elista Ita |date=28 February 2024 |title=Makassar Siap-siap! DAMRI Bakal Sediakan Trayek Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin, Berikut Informasi Rute, Jadwal dan Tarifnya |url=https://www.jawapos.com/infrastruktur/2402280062/makassar-siap-siap-damri-bakal-sediakan-trayek-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-berikut-informasi-rute-jadwal-dan-tarifnya |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=www.jawapos.com |language=id}}</ref> The route is: Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport – DAMRI Daya Pool ticket office – Toddopuli Road – Cappa Bongayya Terminal – Gowa Regency – Takalar Regency – Jeneponto Regency – Bantaeng Regency – Bulukumba Regency – Tanjung Bira.<ref name=":8" /> The service operates daily from both Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport and Tanjung Bira at 20:00 WITA. The journey covers a distance of approximately 205 kilometres, with an estimated travel time of more than five hours. The fare is Rp 200,000.<ref name=":8" />

The local bus rapid transit system, Trans Sulsel, also serves the airport. Corridor 2, which connects [[Hasanuddin University]] and Mandai Railway Station, includes a stop at the airport terminal.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-10-22 |title=Trans Sulsel Gantikan Layanan Teman Bus, Lanjutkan Koridor 1,2 dan 5: Fokus Jaga Konektivitas Antarwilayah |url=https://sulselprov.go.id/post/trans-sulsel-gantikan-layanan-teman-bus-lanjutkan-koridor-1-2-dan-5-fokus-jaga-konektivitas-antarwilayah |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=sulselprov.go.id |language=en}}</ref>

===Car and taxi===
Taxi and shuttle services are available through several companies.

=== Pete-pete ===
A lower-cost public transport option between Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport and Makassar city center is available via [[Share taxi|angkutan kota]] (angkot), locally known as ''pete-pete''. Access to this mode of transport requires exiting the airport premises to Jalan Perintis Kemerdekaan. The distance between the terminal and the airport exit is considerable on foot; however, a free shuttle bus operated at the airport is available for this transfer.<ref name=":9">{{cite web |title=Info Bus Damri Bandara Sultan Hasanuddin Makassar |url=https://www.busbandara.com/info-bus-damri-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-makassar/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190725190448/https://www.busbandara.com/info-bus-damri-bandara-sultan-hasanuddin-makassar/ |archive-date=2019-07-25 |access-date=2015-04-05 |website=busbandara.com |language=id}}</ref>

From the airport exit, ''pete-pete'' services operate toward Daya Terminal, where transfers to other routes bound for the city center are required. The standard fare per ''pete-pete'' journey is approximately Rp4,000, resulting in a total cost of around Rp8,000 for travel between the airport and the city center. This option is generally more economical than taxi services and Damri airport buses, although it involves multiple transfers between vehicles.<ref name=":9" />

Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport (IATA: UPG, ICAO: WAAA) is an international airport serving Makassar, South Sulawesi, Indonesia. The airport is located on the border between Makassar and Maros, a suburb in South Sulawesi, approximately 20 km (12 mi) or 15 minutes from Makassar city center via the freeway/tollway, and about 23 km (14 mi) or 20 minutes via the highway. Named after Sultan Hasanuddin (1631–1670), the Sultan of Gowa and a national hero of Indonesia who resisted the Dutch East India Company in the 1660s, the airport serves as the main gateway to eastern Indonesia and is a major aviation hub in the region. It is the largest airport in eastern Indonesia and one of only three international airports in Sulawesi. The airport serves as a key hub connecting western and eastern Indonesia, offering domestic flights to major cities in western Indonesia such as Jakarta, Surabaya, Denpasar, and Balikpapan, as well as destinations in eastern Indonesia, including Ambon, Ternate, Sorong, and Jayapura. It also provides international connections to destinations such as Singapore and Malaysia. Additionally, the airport is one of the primary embarkation points for Hajj pilgrims from eastern Indonesia, with seasonal flights to Jeddah and Medina.
In addition to serving as a commercial airport, Sultan Hasanuddin International Airport also hosts the Sultan Hasanuddin Air Force Base, a Type-A facility operated by the Indonesian Air Force. It is one of the largest air force bases in eastern Indonesia and is home to four Air Force squadrons: the 5th Reconnaissance Squadron, which operates Boeing 737-200 and CN 235-220 aircraft; the 11th Combat Squadron, equipped with Sukhoi Su-27 and Su-30 fighter jets; the 33rd Transport Squadron, which flies Lockheed C-130H Hercules aircraft; and the 044th Engineering Squadron.
